The XOR Problem

Asking if a game was close or not results in data that is very similar to the XOR problem we saw with perceptrons, where our data is not linearly separable

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
torch.set_printoptions(precision=2)
class SimpleNN(nn.Module):
def __init__(self, input_size, hidden_size, num_classes):
super(SimpleNN, self).__init__()
self.fc1 = nn.Linear(input_size, hidden_size)
self.sig = nn.Sigmoid()
self.fc2 = nn.Linear(hidden_size, num_classes)
def forward(self, x):
z1 = self.fc1(x)
a1 = self.sig(z1)
z2 = self.fc2(a1)
return z2
a.) Draw the computation graph for the network. (4 pts.)
x (2 features) → fc1 (ω1 32×2, b1) → ReLU → fc2 (ω2 16×32, b2) → ReLU → fc3 (ω3 1×16, b3) → sigmoid → ŷ → BCE (with the label y) → L. Each weight matrix and bias is an input to its Linear node.
b.) Give the loss of the neural network (L) as a single statement of nested functions. (1 pt.)
L = BCE(σ(relu(relu(x ω1T + b1) ω2T + b2) ω3T + b3), y)

Condensing the Hidden Layer

We can compactly represent the operations of the hidden layer as a single matrix multiplication.

Z1 = Xω1T + b1
A1 = σ(Z1)

Weights as Matrices: Equation Conventions

There are a number of different conventions for writing the linear transformation as used in a linear_layer. I use a slightly non-standard one that I believe maps better to PyTorch and the diagrams I show in class.

ConventionEquationWhere you'll see it
Bias folded inZ = Xω
(X gets a column of 1s)		Linear regression, perceptrons and SVMs
Inputs × outputsZ = Xω + bKeras/TensorFlow, many textbooks
Outputs × inputsZ = XωT + bPyTorch nn.Linear and this course

PyTorch stores one row per neuron so it reads like the math: XωT + b

Backpropagation · Review09

Improving the Weights

Linear Regressions and OLS

Due to the simplicity of linear regression, we could use a closed-form solution (OLS) to directly find the optimal set of weights.

This is due to the loss function (SSE) being perfectly convex

Backpropagation · Gradient Descent10

Gradient Descent

Gradient Descent is an optimization method that iteratively tries to find a set of values (weights) that minimize the loss (cost) function

A gradient is the slope of a curve at a given point in a specified direction

In the case of a univariate function, it is simply the first derivative at a selected point.

Backpropagation · Gradient Descent11

Multivariate Gradient Descent

In the case of a multivariate function, the gradient is a vector of partial derivatives (one per variable)

Backpropagation · Gradient Descent12

Quasi-Convex Functions

We can also use quasi-convex functions with gradient descent, but need to watch out for local minima (and flat spots)

Backpropagation · Gradient Descent13

Gradient Descent Algorithm

\omega_{new} = \omega_{old} - \alpha\,\frac{\partial J}{\partial \omega}

Backpropagation · Backpropagation17

Backpropagation (Backprop)

Backpropagation is a technique in deep learning to compute the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight for a network.

Backprop is a method (the chain rule, applied backward) that allows us to implement Gradient Descent for multi-layer models

Backpropagation · Backpropagation18

Computational Graphs

Every network can be represented by a computational graph, or a graph of the operations happening to the input as it passes through the network

Backpropagation · Backpropagation19

The Chain Rule

The chain rule enables us to find derivatives of composite (nested) functions!

\frac{d}{dx}\left[f(g(x))\right] = f'(g(x))\,g'(x)

import torch
class LinearLayer:
def __init__(self, n_in, n_out):
self.W = torch.randn(n_out, n_in) * (2/n_in)**0.5
self.b = torch.zeros(n_out)
def forward(self, X):
self.X = X # keep for backward
return X @ self.W.T + self.b
def backward(self, dY):
self.dW = dY.T @ self.X # dL/dW
self.db = dY.sum(dim=0) # dL/db
return dY @ self.W # dL/dX, sent down
def update(self, lr):
self.W -= lr * self.dW
self.b -= lr * self.db

def backward(self, logits, y):
grad = loss_grad(logits, y) # dL/dlogits
for layer in reversed(self.layers): # chain rule
grad = layer.backward(grad) # back to front
def update(self, lr):
for layer in self.layers:
layer.update(lr)

Backprop Exercise (old final exam question)

a.) Draw the computation graph for the network. (4 pts.)
x (784) → lin1 (ω1 100×784, b1) → z1 → ReLU → a1 → lin2 (ω2 10×100, b2) → z2 → softmax → ŷ → cross-entropy (with y) → L.
b.) Give the derivative chain for calculating the gradient of the bias in the first layer. (3 pts.)
∂L/∂b1 = ∂L/∂z2 · ∂z2/∂a1 · ∂a1/∂z1 · ∂z1/∂b1 = (ŷ − y) ω2 ⊙ relu′(z1) · 1, where relu′(z1) is 1 where z1 > 0 and 0 elsewhere.
d.) Given the gradients, what’s the next step we should take? (1 pt.)
Take a gradient descent step: move every weight and bias against its gradient, ω ← ω − α ∂L/∂ω (in PyTorch, optimizer.step() after loss.backward(), then zero the gradients).
e.) What task could this network be used for? (Hint: It’s something I used as an example a lot) (1 pt.)
Classifying MNIST handwritten digits: 784 inputs are the 28 × 28 pixels of an image, and the 10 outputs are the digits 0 to 9.

Binary stepf(x) = 0 for x < 0, 1 for x ≥ 0

f′(x) = f(x)(1 − f(x))

Backpropagation · Backpropagation25

On the exam…

NameEquation and derivative
Mean Squared Error (MSE)L = (1/n) Σ (y − ŷ)2
∂L/∂ŷ = −2(y − ŷ)
Mean Absolute Error (MAE)L = (1/n) Σ |y − ŷ|
∂L/∂ŷ = −sign(y − ŷ)
Huber LossL = 0.5(y − ŷ)2 if |y − ŷ| ≤ δ, else δ(|y − ŷ| − 0.5δ)
piecewise gradient
Binary Cross Entropy (BCE)L = −[y log(ŷ) + (1 − y) log(1 − ŷ)]
∂L/∂ŷ = (ŷ − y) / (ŷ(1 − ŷ))

On the exam…

NameEquation and derivative
BCE with SigmoidL = −[y log(σ(z)) + (1 − y) log(1 − σ(z))]
∂L/∂z = σ(z) − y
Categorical Cross EntropyL = −Σi yi log(ŷi)
∂L/∂zj = ŷj − yj (with ŷ = softmax(z))
KL DivergenceL = Σ y log(y / ŷ)
∂L/∂ŷ = −y / ŷ
Poisson LossL = ŷ − y log(ŷ)
∂L/∂ŷ = 1 − y / ŷ

Some Issues with Backprop

There are some issues that appear when you start using backprop:

  • Vanishing gradients
  • Exploding gradients
Backpropagation · Issues with Backprop28

Vanishing Gradient

Since you are multiplying increasingly small values with each other during backprop, the gradient eventually trends to 0, meaning updates will stop happening.

Backpropagation · Issues with Backprop29

Vanishing Gradient

Backpropagation · Issues with Backprop30

Exploding Gradient

Almost the opposite of the vanishing gradient, the exploding gradient is when the gradients become too large, so the weights take huge steps and the loss blows up

Backpropagation · Issues with Backprop31

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
import torch.optim as optim
class Net(nn.Module):
def __init__(self):
super().__init__()
self.fc1 = nn.Linear(784, 100)
self.fc2 = nn.Linear(100, 10)
def forward(self, x):
return self.fc2(F.relu(self.fc1(x)))
# Initialize network, optimizer and device (GPU)
device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available()
else "cpu")
network = Net().to(device)
optimizer = optim.SGD(network.parameters(), lr=0.01,
momentum=0.5)
